title: Steven Spielberg Says Aliens Have Already Visited Earth. His New Film Drops in India Thursday.
excerpt: Disclosure Day is the director's first original sci-fi since E.T. in 1982 — and early word calls it his best work in two decades. Emily Blunt and Josh O'Connor lead what might be this summer's most important film.
body:
There is a version of this story where Steven Spielberg is 79 years old and coasting. He's made West Side Story, he's made The Fabelmans, he has nothing left to prove to anyone. He could direct prestige dramas until the industry gives him a lifetime achievement Oscar and calls it a career.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=SCYT8vb2siQ

Instead, the man went back to aliens.

Disclosure Day arrives in Indian theatres this Thursday, June 12 — the same day as Main Vaapas Aaunga and Governor, because June 2026 apparently has no chill — and it marks Spielberg's first original science fiction film since E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial in 1982. Let that sink in. Forty-four years between original sci-fi stories. Every alien film he's made since then — War of the Worlds, Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull, even Ready Player One in a loose sense — was based on someone else's material. This one is his.

The Story

The premise is deceptively simple: a young cybersecurity expert named Daniel Kellner (played by the magnetic Josh O'Connor, fresh off his Crown-era stardom) gets his hands on evidence that extraterrestrial life exists. He wants to tell the world. Powerful people want him silenced. Standing between them is Margaret Fairchild, a Kansas City meteorologist and former journalist played by Emily Blunt, who may be the only person willing to help him get the truth out.

Colin Firth plays the head of a shadowy corporation. Colman Domingo plays a defector from within. Wyatt Russell and Eve Hewson round out a cast so stacked it reads like a prestige drama that wandered into a summer tentpole slot.

The screenplay comes from David Koepp, Spielberg's long-time collaborator — the man who wrote Jurassic Park, The Lost World, and War of the Worlds. This is their first original project together. No franchise. No adaptation. Just two veterans with something to say about what happens when the truth is too big for the people in charge.

Spielberg Believes

In a CBS Sunday Morning interview that went immediately viral, Spielberg dropped any pretence of ambiguity about his personal views:

"Based on the circumstantial evidence of everything that I've gathered throughout my whole life — everybody I've listened to, every documentary I've ever watched, and all the testimonies in Congress that I've heard — I absolutely think that they have been here, and they are here. And who knows, maybe they've always been here."

This isn't marketing. This is a man who has spent five decades making films about contact, wonder, and what happens when humanity confronts something beyond itself — and he's saying the quiet part out loud. Whether you find that thrilling or slightly unhinged, it charges every frame of Disclosure Day with an urgency his recent work hasn't had.

What We're Hearing

Early impressions have been rapturous. Screen Rant called it his "best film in 20 years." The Rotten Tomatoes prediction is sky-high. Josh O'Connor, in a Filmfare exclusive, described Spielberg as "more spontaneous than people realise" — a director who lets the set inspire the shot rather than predetermining every angle. "He is really all about the actors and working with them to bring a story to life," O'Connor said.

At 145 minutes, it's a long sit — but this is Spielberg. The man doesn't waste screen time.

The Diaspora Angle

For NRI audiences, Disclosure Day lands in a peculiar sweet spot. It's competing for screens against two major Hindi releases on the same date, which means Indian theatres will be splitting attention. But Spielberg remains event cinema in India — the kind of name that fills IMAX screens regardless of what else is playing.

The film releases in English with subtitles across major Indian multiplexes. No Hindi dub has been announced, which may limit its reach in single-screen markets but won't matter in the metros and overseas, where the diaspora audience treats a new Spielberg the way previous generations treated a new Yash Chopra: as appointment viewing.

The Bottom Line

The man who made Close Encounters of the Third Kind, E.T., and Jurassic Park is 79 years old and still reaching for the sky. Literally. Disclosure Day isn't a victory lap — it's a provocation. A filmmaker who changed how we imagine aliens is now saying, on camera, that he thinks they're real.

If the film delivers on even half of what the early buzz suggests, Thursday night in a dark theatre might be the most Spielbergian experience we've had in a generation.
